title: Comparing and ordering rational numbers
blurb: Put any mix of fractions, decimals, percents and negatives in order, and pick the right inequality symbol every time.
question: Your practice scores are 42/50 in reading, 0.83 in math and 85% in science. Which is your strongest section, and how do you order the three scores from least to greatest?

teach.body: Formally, a rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction a/b of integers with b ≠ 0, so fractions, terminating and repeating decimals, percents and their negatives all count. To compare them, put them in the same form. In plain English: you can't fairly compare 3/8 with 41% until both are decimals (0.375 and 0.41). Then compare place by place.

head: Symbol or word
Meaning
Example
teach.caption: The symbol's open side faces the larger number.

items: Write back in the original forms: 0.58, 3/5, 61%, 5/8.
Check two neighbors by cross-multiplying: 3/5 vs 5/8 → 3 × 8 = 24 < 5 × 5 = 25, so 3/5 < 5/8. ✓

teach.caption: More digits does not mean bigger: the first place that differs decides.

items: Same numerator: the LARGER denominator is the SMALLER fraction (smaller pieces). 1/8 < 1/6.

teach.body: On a number line, values increase to the right, so a negative number closer to 0 is GREATER. −0.5 > −0.75 even though 0.75 > 0.5, and −1/3 > −1/2. Any positive number is greater than any negative number. When ordering negatives, think "owing money": owing $0.50 is better than owing $0.75.

teach.text: The TEAS builds wrong orderings from: "more digits is bigger" (0.125 > 0.2), "bigger denominator is bigger" (1/8 > 1/6), ordering negatives by size (−0.75 > −0.5), comparing 45% with 0.5 as "45 is bigger", and giving the list in descending order when ascending was asked.

teach.h: Scenario: Kevin ranks his practice scores
teach.body: Kevin Nguyen scored 42/50 in reading, 0.83 in math and 85% in science. Convert: 42 ÷ 50 = 0.84; 0.83 stays; 85% = 0.85. Pad and compare: 0.83 < 0.84 < 0.85. Least to greatest: math (0.83), reading (42/50), science (85%). His strongest section is science and his weakest is math. Check: 42/50 = 84/100 = 84%, between 83% and 85%. ✓

items: Convert to one form (usually decimals), pad with zeros, compare from the left.
Same numerator: larger denominator means smaller fraction; otherwise cross-multiply.
For negatives, closer to 0 is greater.
Read the direction: ascending is least to greatest; descending is greatest to least.

summary: You can now compare and order any mix of fractions, decimals, percents and negative numbers by converting to one form and comparing place by place. You avoid the digit-count, denominator, negative-number and direction traps the TEAS sets.

A.q: Which list orders 0.4, 3/8, 0.38 and 41% from least to greatest?

whyNot.0: This treats numbers with more digits as larger (0.4, then 0.38 and 0.41, then 0.375); padded, 0.400 is greater than 0.380 and 0.375.
whyNot.1: This is greatest to least, the descending order.
whyNot.3: This treats 0.38 as larger than 0.4 because 38 > 4; compare tenths first: 3 < 4.

whyNot.2: 0.07 = 0.07 and 0.7 = 0.70; 7 hundredths is less than 70 hundredths.

A.q: Which fraction has the greatest value?

whyNot.2: 9/16 has the largest numerator and denominator but the smallest value, 0.5625.

B.q: Which list orders −0.3, −0.25, −1/3 and −2/5 from greatest to least?

whyNot.0: This is least to greatest; it is the same as ordering the negatives by size.
whyNot.1: This treats 0.25 as larger than 0.3 because 25 > 3, so −0.25 is placed below −0.3.
whyNot.2: This treats 1/3 as smaller than 0.3, but 1/3 = 0.333..., so −1/3 is less than −0.3.

B.q: Four clinics report the share of staff who got a flu shot: A 0.68, B 2/3, C 67.5%, D 13/20. Which clinic has the highest rate?

whyNot.2: 67.5% = 0.675, which is less than 0.680; it looks bigger only if 67.5 is compared with 0.68 unconverted.

B.q: Four patients each drank part of a 1-liter bottle: 5/16, 1/3, 3/11 and 2/7 of the bottle. Which amount is the least?

whyNot.0: 5/16 has the largest denominator, but its value (0.3125) is not the least.
whyNot.1: 1/3 has the smallest numerator, but at 0.333 it is the greatest of the four.

C.q: Which list orders 1.45, 7/5, 135% and 1 3/8 from least to greatest?

whyNot.0: This treats 135% as 135 instead of 1.35, putting it last.
whyNot.2: This converts 7/5 as 5 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.71, dividing the wrong way; 7/5 = 1.4.
whyNot.3: This is greatest to least, the descending order.

whyNot.0: 0.305 has more digits but is less than 0.35 (0.305 < 0.350).
whyNot.2: 0.43 is just above 3/7 ≈ 0.4286, so it is outside the range.

C.q: Practice-test scores: Ana 17/20, Ben 0.8, Cara 83%, Dev 5/6. Which lists the students from highest to lowest score?

whyNot.1: This is lowest to highest, the reverse of what was asked.
whyNot.2: This puts 83% above 5/6, but 5/6 = 0.8333... is slightly more than 0.83.
whyNot.3: This compares 83% as the number 83 without converting, so Cara jumps to first.

reteach.title: Ordering is like comparing prices
reteach.question: If one store says $0.4, another says 38 cents, and a third says 3/8 of a dollar, how do you find the cheapest?

blocks.body: Prices only compare fairly in one unit. $0.4 is 40 cents, 38 cents stays 38, and 3/8 of a dollar is 37.5 cents. Now it is obvious: 37.5 < 38 < 40. Converting to decimals and padding with zeros is the same move: 0.375, 0.380, 0.400. And debt works the other way: owing 38 cents is better (greater) than owing 40 cents, which is why −0.38 > −0.4.

items: Convert each value to the same form (cents, or decimals).
Line them up with the same number of places.
Compare from the left; for debts (negatives), smaller debt is greater.

blocks.text: $0.4 is not 4 cents. Padding it to $0.40 shows it is the most expensive of the three.

explain.body: Pad with zeros so every decimal has the same number of places, then compare from the left. The first place that differs decides.

test.why: Padded: 0.3070, 0.3007, 0.3700, 0.0730. Tenths: 3, 3, 3, 0; hundredths of the 3s: 0, 0, 7. So 0.37 is greatest.

whyNot.0: 0.307 = 0.3070, smaller than 0.3700 in the hundredths place (0 < 7).
whyNot.1: 0.3007 has the most digits but is the second smallest.
whyNot.3: 0.073 has 0 tenths, so it is the smallest.

explain.body: For a/b vs c/d, compare a × d with b × c. The bigger cross-product sits with the bigger fraction. 7/9 vs 4/5: 7 × 5 = 35 and 9 × 4 = 36.

whyNot.1: > would need 7/9 to be larger, but 0.777... is less than 0.8.
whyNot.3: ≥ means greater than or equal; 7/9 is neither.

explain.body: Convert, then picture the number line. −2/3 ≈ −0.667 and −0.7 = −0.700. −0.667 is closer to 0, so it is greater.

test.q: Which number is greater, −2/3 or −0.7, and why?

whyNot.0: A bigger size makes a negative number SMALLER: 0.7 > 0.667 means −0.7 < −0.667.
whyNot.2: −0.7 is farther from 0 than −0.667, not closer.
whyNot.3: 2/3 = 0.666..., which is not equal to 0.7; rounding to one place hides the difference.

explain.body: Convert percents (÷ 100) and fractions (top ÷ bottom) to decimals, order them, then read the question again: descending means greatest first.

test.q: Which list orders 0.09, 9.5%, 1/12 and 0.1 in descending order?

whyNot.0: This is ascending order (least to greatest).
whyNot.1: This treats 9.5% as 9.5 rather than 0.095, putting it first.
whyNot.3: This converts 9.5% to 0.0095 (point moved 3 places), putting it last.
